overview: These historical Senegal labels cover changing regional and colonial footprints. The 1530 outline stretches far south beyond modern Senegal and does not establish a unified state or a French colony at that date. Later snapshots narrow to coastal Senegal; the 1900 record represents colonial territory. This phased narrative follows documented communities and institutions, while the modern republic has its own card.

periods.title: An imprecise early map label
periods.summary: The broad imported footprint is not evidence of one unified Senegalese state.

periods.title: Trading settlements and expanding colonial influence
periods.summary: Saint-Louis grew from a French trading settlement among existing coastal communities.

periods.title: Colonial Senegal in French West Africa
periods.summary: Colonial institutions, transport and urban politics shaped these later snapshots.

items.text: A French chartered company established itself at Saint-Louis in 1659. Traders used the Senegal River to seek gum arabic, hides, gold and enslaved people. The island settlement depended on waterways and surrounding communities; its commercial importance should not be mistaken for French control of the whole region.

Historian Alain Sinou emphasizes African and mixed-ancestry merchants in the settlement’s development. Saint-Louis had neither farmland nor a freshwater source sufficient for its needs, so its survival depended on mainland supplies and negotiated relationships. The river was a route to dinner and drinking water as well as to commercial cargo.

Some signares, women of property in Saint-Louis and Gorée, controlled substantial houses and commercial wealth. Scholarship also records their ownership of enslaved domestic workers. Their influence challenges a history that notices only European men, while the labour supporting affluent households must remain visible too.

Surviving Saint-Louis houses reveal practical design choices. Shops occupied large ground-floor rooms, while upper rooms had high wooden ceilings and many openings. Balconies and broad verandas created shaded space. The city’s heritage description helps explain how trade, household life and the search for cooler air could share one building.

Roger Pasquier’s study of food supply from 1840 to 1870 describes millet used for couscous and sanglé, alongside wheat flour for bread and rice eaten across communities. Rice became especially useful when millet was scarce. Feeding a town meant organizing trade and transport, not simply growing food inside its boundaries.

Enslaved families also acted to change their lives. Research on liberation registers from 1857 to 1903 identifies adults and children who fled together to demand freedom. Ninety percent of the family units identified in that study were headed by women. Family attachment could become a reason to take enormous risks together.

“Grammaire de la langue woloffe” means “Grammar of the Wolof Language.” This French title appears on P.-David Boilat’s 1858 book, published by the Imprimerie Impériale. The title is an attested sample of writing from the period; its historical spelling of “woloffe” is retained rather than silently modernized.

European print was only one route into writing. Boston University’s Ajami research documents African languages written in adapted Arabic scripts and the preservation of Wolof manuscripts. These traditions remind us to look beyond French-language books when asking who studied, composed texts or passed knowledge between generations.

A teacher-training college was created at Saint-Louis by an order of 24 November 1903. The institution later known as William Ponty trained educators for French West Africa. Its much later student papers, beginning in 1933, preserved studies of community life: that documentary legacy continued beyond this map record’s 1914 endpoint.

The Faidherbe Bridge’s spans arrived from France in separate pieces in 1897. The bridge joined a city already organized around quays and river crossings. UNESCO dates its inauguration to 19 October: engineering altered movement around Saint-Louis while the older street pattern remained recognizable.

The Dakar to Saint-Louis railway was completed in 1885. Research traces how it drew merchants, migrant workers, formerly enslaved people and farmers into the peanut-growing region. Rails carried crops toward markets, but their social effects depended on the people who moved, worked and traded along them.

Peanut production involved much more than harvesting a field. Cropper’s study describes women sowing, weeding and shelling, while migrant farm workers also grew crops or sold charcoal on their own account. Peanuts supplied food and livestock feed, and their byproducts could become fuel. Almost every part of the crop acquired a job.

Saint-Louis remained a major colonial centre, but its role changed when Dakar became the capital of French West Africa in 1902. Senegal’s own colonial capital stayed at Saint-Louis much longer. One city losing a particular administrative title did not mean its households, crafts or trade disappeared.

Blaise Diagne won election as Senegal’s deputy on 10 May 1914. His campaign called for a lycée, teacher-training and medical schools in Dakar, and defended freedom of religious conscience. The demands show education and health as political questions, not simply gifts that colonial officials decided to distribute.

A bubonic-plague epidemic struck Dakar in 1914. Colonial officials blamed African residents, expelled people from the centre and burned homes. Historian Tobias Warner connects these measures to the creation of the segregated Médina neighbourhood. An epidemic became a struggle over who could live where, and on what terms.

Residents resisted through a general strike, political action and street protest. Their response makes the history of sanitation more than a story of official orders: people argued about what protection should mean and about the destruction of their homes. Médina later became an important place of cultural creativity.

ending.text: The imported endpoints of 1878 and 1914 mark map coverage, not the extinction of Senegalese communities or the end of French rule. Colonial rule continued into the twentieth century; Senegal’s independence and the dissolution of the Mali Federation came in 1960.
